children.notes: Let's learn the Caro-Kann! This opening was invented in 1886 by GM Levy Rozman and remains one of the best counter attacks to white playing pawn e4. OK, not all of that is true, but let's start with playing with pawn to c6.
White is greedy taking the whole center, now we fight back with pawn to d5. White has a choice here - do they take? Do they push? Or do they ignore?

White chose to push their pawn, bringing us to the caro-kann advanced variation. This is the most popular move by White, probably because they are too scared to take. The truth is they should be scared to play us in general, because we've studied every possible response. Let's play pawn to c5 immediately, trying to destabilize the center.
White is greedy and took our pawn. Let's immediately attack their weak pawns with knight to c6.
Taking the pawn back on e5 is actually a bit poisonous. Let's continue with our regular play: Pawn to e6, opening up our bishop and giving our knight a way to develop.
We still shouldn't take the pawn. Instead, pawn to a5.
Finally!!! Black made a mistake. NOW we can take the pawn. Knight to e5.
White's bishop is powerful right now. The best move to fight back is pawn to f6.
And we take back of course! Pawn takes on e5
Oh no a check!!!! Actually white is playing awful here and we have a huge advantage. Let's play pawn to g6.
Finally, knight to f6.
Well done!! Even though we are down a pawn, We are definitely winning one back soon and our strong center means the computer gives us a 2 or 3 point advantage!!
If they don't take us, we'll take them. Pawn takes on b4.
And now rook takes rook on a1.
YES! Now we get our pawn back. Knight takes pawn on b4.
Well done!! The computer loves our position here, and white bishop is stuck staring at his pawn.
This was a very strong response from white, actually. I wouldn't have guessed the next move in a million years. It's knight h6. I'm not going to even try and explain that one to you.
White is playing well here. Let's play the classic pawn to e6.
Now we can fight back against White's strong pawns with pawn to a5.
Let's unpin with bishop to d7.
Take back of course. Bishop to c6.
Because White's king is so weak, the computer gives us a 1 or 2 point advantage from this position.
As usual, when the knight comes out we want to pin him. Bishop to g4
Ah now we see the point of our knight on h6. We can hop into f5 to attack the bishop. OK that wasn't so hard.
White's pawns are looking a little too stable. Let's cause some chaos with pawn to g5.
Now look at this cool move. With 1 pawn push we will attack 2 undefended pawns. Pawn to e6.
That was cool! Now our queen looks at the pawn on g5 and the bishop looks at the pawn on c5. We are going to get our material back!
Now our favorite move; pawn to e6, opening up an attack on the undefended c5 pawn.
Now knight to f5, hitting the bishop.
Well done! Black wins most of their games from this position.
Let's switch our focus to attacking the other pawn with pawn to e6. This opens up our bishop to attack the c5 pawn, and gives our knight a path for developing.
White is trying to stabilize their pawn, so let's destabilize. Pawn to a5.
And now pawn takes b4, opening up our rook.
Last thing: let's unpin our selves with bishop to d7. Now that the knight is unpinned, the pawn on b4 is technically under attack.
And we take back. Bishop takes c6.
Well done! We'll continue with our regular development from here.
Let's take back of course. Pawn takes on c6.
Very common move in this type of position: pawn to a5.
And then we take with pawn to b4.
Now the very fun queen to h4. The point is we are attacking the b4 pawn, but also have some tricky checks up our sleeve.
Now for our tricky check: queen to e4 forking the king, the g2 pawn, AND the e5 pawn.
Do NOT trade queens here. Queen to g2.
And now our queen retreats to g6.

Well done! We are doing great here! Look how weak and exposed White's king is. There is nowhere for him to hide. As long as we keep our queen on the board, White has problems. Meanwhile, all our pawns are connected and coordinated
OK now let's develop and route our knight as planned. Knight to e7.
And now the knight ends up on his home on f5, attacking the bishop.
White plays that move 90% of the time. If we take, we help their pawn structure, so we wont take. Instead, let's unpin our king with bishop to d7.
Well done! We have a solid position position and are ready to finish developing and castle.
White wants to defend their pawns, but we won't make it so easy for them. Bishop to g4.
Let's toss in a check with queen to a5.
Now we can play pawn to e6. This stabilizes our center, opens up our bishop to attack the pawn on c5, and gives our knight a path to develop.
Well done! We have a chess game ahead of us.
White once again rejects taking our pawn, and from here we will win lots of games. Knight to c6 immediately, adding more pressure to the d4 pawn.
We're going to get this position a LOT. Let's slightly clarify the situation with pawn takes pawn on d4.
The d4 pawn is now White's biggest weakness. Our game plan: attack this pawn with everything we have. Let's develop our bishop to g4, pinning the knight to remove a defender of the d4 pawn.
This mindless move from white gives us a huge edge. Bishop takes knight on f3.
Now we just have knight takes d4, attacking the queen.
Let's bring our knight back to c6.
Beautiful! We are simply up a pawn.
Let's bring our queen out to b6, adding yet another attacker to the d4 pawn.
Well done! White has a really hard time defending their position here.
Let's play pawn to e6. This move opens up our bishop, and also opens up the e7 square for our knight on the next move. Right now our knight is kind of trapped at home.
This is just a bad move from white, plain and simply. When White plays h3, we take the knight on f3, removing a defender of the d4 pawn.

Now we get queen to b6, adding another attacker to the d4 pawn. Also kind of cool: queen to b6 is only possible because we moved our c pawn at the start of the game! If we didn't, she would be blocked in. Funny how that works.
White saved one pawn but now loses another. Queen takes b2.
Let's develop our bishop to b4, pinning the knight to the king.
Well done! We are up a pawn and have a very playable position.
Let's starting routing our knight to his new home. First, knight to e7.
Then, knight to f5. Now we are putting even more pressure on that weak d4 pawn.
Dang, White really wants to defend that pawn. Their bishop has turned into a glorified pawn now. Let's continue developing, putting our bishop on his home on e7.
Let's castle
Well done! We have a good position here.
Now we take the knight! The knight is one of the last defenders of that weak d4 pawn, so we are very happy to remove it. Bishop takes f3.
Let's take a moment to castle here.
We have one pawn-break in our pocket, and now is a good time to use it. Pawn to f6.
White took! Which means we can play bishop to f6, adding yet ANOTHER attacker to the weak d4 pawn.
Well done! This is a great position to play as black. All our pieces are aligned towards White's biggest weakness.
Has white moved like... a single piece this game? I don't think so. Anyways, pawn takes on d4.

OK let's play a move you've never played before: pawn to h5. The point is... well the point is pretty complicated. Something about strengthening our light squares yada yada yada. All I know is black wins most of their games when they play pawn to h5.
OK let's pin the knight. Bishop to g4.
Now that our bishop is developed, we can play pawn to e6.
The last step is to develop our queen to b6.
Well done! Even though the material is equal, the computer thinks we are better in this position.
White pins our knight? Let's pin White's pawn. Queen to a5. Now White has to decide what to do with their bishop.
Of course we take back. Pawn takes on c6.
White is threatening a discovered attack on our queen. We need to retreat, while still keeping the defense of our c5 pawn. Let's do so with queen to b6.
Well done! We are better in this position. And we have ideas of bishop to a6 in the future.

Our mission: attack that bishop. 
Our method: use our king's knight.
Our first step: knight to h6 to eventually go to f5.
White took our knight to double up our pawns. We really have no choice. Pawn takes bishop on h6.
Now the always fun queen to b6.
Well done! We have a ton of threats on white and it'll be hard for our opponent to deal with them. Black wins over 60% of the time from this position.
This time white decides to take our pawn, taking us into the exchanged variation. Let's take back with pawn to d5.
This is the start of the Panov-Botvinnik Attack. The name doesn't matter, what matters is developing and strengthening the center. Knight to f6.
Honestly, that d4 pawn looks a bit weak. Let's play pawn to g6, with the idea to place our bishop on g7 on our next move to stare down at that d-pawn.
We continue with out plan: bishop to g7.
White wanted to trade pawns? OK. Knight takes back on d5.
Our knight is under attack. We can either retreat or trade, and I don't believe in retreating. Knight takes on c3.
The bishop on c4 is unprotected, and the pawn on c3 is unprotected. We can attack both with queen to c7. White will lose one of them.
Well done! We are putting serious pressure on White with our queen. The computer thinks we have a better position here.
If White wants to trade, we trade. Knight takes back on d5.
Let's continue developing and apply a bit of pressure on the center with knight to c6.
Let's continue with bishop to f5, piercing through White's queenside.
We have two attackers on our knight. Let's defend with pawn to e6.
Well done! We have a solid position here.
This is a sharp line from white. Let's exploit the fact that his pawn is unprotected with knight to c6.
Let's continue with the other knight. Knight to f6. This will also allow us to develop our bishop to g4 in the future.
White wasted some time there trying to thwart our bishop. Let's go aggressive with pawn to e5.
And now we take with the knight. Knight to e5.
Well done! We have a good position and are ready to continue our game.
Remember we developed the knight so we can put the bishop on g4. Well let's do that! Bishop to g4.
White escaped, and is now threatening our b7 pawn. Let's defend with queen to d7.
The last piece we need to develop is the bishop. Let's play pawn to e6 to open it up.
White's dark-square bishop is better than ours. Let's go for a trade with bishop to d6.
Now queen takes back on d6.
Let's castle kingside too.
Well done navigating the caro kann main line!! Proud of you.
Let's copy white with knight to f6.
With white developing their bishop so early, we have the opportunity to pin the knight. Bishop pins the knight on g4.
Let's get our other knight into the game and attack the now-undefended pawn on d4. Knight to c6.
Now we want our other bishop in the game. Let's open it up with pawn to e6.
We should keep the pin and drop our bishop back to h5.
The best move here is bishop to d6.
Let's force White's bishop back with pawn to h6.
And now the key: Queen to c7, setting up a battery.
Well done! The computer likes our position here, and  black wins something like 60% of the time from this position.
Let's unpin ourselves with bishop to e7.
Finally, we can castle kingside.
White set up a battery on our h7 pawn. Let's push it to h6 so it doesn't get taken.
Now let's go rook to c8 - it may not be attacking the queen just yet but give it a few moves and you'll be glad you did it.
Well done! The position is equal and we are ready to play!
If White doesn't move their pawn, then fine, we'll take them instead. Pawn takes on e4.
Let's develop the knight with knight to f6.
White declined taking our knight. Let's send a pawn up to ask him why. Pawn to h5.
With White's h-pawn out of the way, we can target White's queen with bishop to g4.
Now our tried & true pawn to e6 to open up our bishop.
Let's develop our bishop to d6, attacking White's the very unstable kingside.
Well done! We are threatening to take White's knight and double his pawns. The computer is giving us the edge in this position.
Our pawn continues! Pawn to h4.
Finally let's put our bishop on g4.
Well done! Black wins most games from this position.
If White takes our knight we enter a very fun line. First step, we take back with our e-pawn! e-pawn takes on f6.
Let's develop our bishop with a plan to castle kingside. Bishop to d6.
Now we can castle.
White is threatening some annoying stuff with their queen and bishop pointed at h7. Let's throw in a check before we do anything else. Rook to e8.
OK let's stop our pawn from getting captured with pawn to h5.
White developed their bishop because they are going to castle queenside. When players castle on opposite sides, that means a war is brewing. Let's play knight to d7.
One last thing before the war breaks out: knight to f8. This protects the crucial h7 square. As they say: "Knight on f8, never mate"
Well done! The positions are equal and we are ready to play a fantastic game of chess. Everything we did was theory by the way: this exact position has been reached a hundred thousand times!
White castled directly into our pawn. Interesting. Let's push our pawn forward to h4.
Now let's develop our knight and bring him over to help defend our king. Knight to d7.
And the knight completes his journey with knight to f8
Well done! The stage is set and the game can begin!
Knight to f3 is a slow move. Let's develop our bishop and prepare to castle. Bishop to d6.
Let's castle
Now we should take the open file with our rook. Rook to e8.
Our next plan is to route our knight all the way to the king. Every marathon starts with a step. Knight to d7.
Second step of our marathon: Knight to f8.
OK turns out the marathon was only two steps. Black wins something like 60% of the time from this position. Good luck!
